content: Trench mouth, also known as necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG), is a polymicrobial infection of the gums. It is characterized by inflammation, bleeding, deep ulcerations, necrosis of gum tissue, and, in some cases, fever. The condition is caused by an overgrowth of bacteria that are normally present in the mouth. This bacterial overpopulation is often triggered by factors such as poor oral hygiene, an inadequate diet, smoking, or the presence of other infections. The primary causative organisms include anaerobic bacteria like Bacteroides and Fusobacterium, as well as spirochetes such as Borrelia and Treponema species. Differentiating trench mouth from other diseases is critical. The most important differential diagnosis is primary herpetic gingivostomatitis. Additionally, it is necessary to distinguish necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG) from acute herpetic gingivostomatitis. In terms of clinical findings, trench mouth may present with a grayish film on the gums, which is caused by decomposed gum tissue. Patients may also experience fever and swollen lymph nodes in the head and neck region. A throat swab culture can be performed to aid in diagnosis. Dental x-rays or facial x-rays may be utilized to assess the severity of the infection and to determine the extent of tissue destruction. These imaging studies help guide the management and treatment of the condition.
